title: Natural Resources in Shinnecock Elders’ Knowledge (2014)
summary: A page-cited guide to Shinnecock elders’ knowledge of plants, animals, food, materials, language, and remembered resource places.
content:
Fish returning in spring, reeds woven into homes, berries shared in kitchens, and wildlife living alongside the community: the Shinnecock Environmental Department’s 2014 catalogue connects natural resources with everyday work and knowledge.

Read the original catalogue

Shinnecock Environmental Department, Natural Resources Identified by Shinnecock Elders, April 4, 2014, PDF p. 1. Page numbers count the cover as PDF page 1. The 23-page scan has no printed page numbers; citations here use PDF page order, including the cover.

The catalogue combines Shinnecock elders’ memories and community knowledge with a reference list. Historical uses are not modern medical or foraging advice. Names and remembered places are preserved with their uncertainties; a 2014 location entry does not establish present abundance or public access.

Reading names and uncertainty

The catalogue’s spellings belong to this source. “Matcik” appears with turtles, “Autuk” with deer, “Skuk” with snakes, and “Chunckoo” with oysters. Its proposed raccoon word carries a question mark. Manittuwond is an island name on the beach-plum page, not a plant translation. Read the language section for the full distinctions.

The cranberry page mixes remembered cranberries with highbush-cranberry names; the peach page labels persimmon only as a possibility. The shark, bass, and snake lists also need taxonomic care. Medicinal statements are evidence of recorded traditions, not proof of effectiveness.

Shinnecock Environmental Department, Natural Resources Identified by Shinnecock Elders, April 4, 2014, PDF pp. 1–23. Page numbers count the cover as PDF page 1.
